title: Two black holes merged and turned about three Suns’ worth of mass into ripples in space

cover.alt: Aerial view of the LIGO Hanford Observatory: a long straight arm running for kilometres across flat brown desert from a cluster of buildings.

body: On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO detectors, at Hanford and Livingston in the US, picked up a signal that lasted about a fifth of a second. It came from two black holes, of about 36 and 29 times the Sun’s mass, spiralling together some 1.4 billion light-years away into one of about 62. The missing mass, about **3 Suns’ worth**, left as gravitational waves: ripples in space-time that stretch and squeeze whatever they pass through. Each detector catches them by bouncing laser light along two 4 km arms and watching for tiny changes in their length.

slides.question: The detectors are 3,002 km apart. How many milliseconds after Livingston did Hanford see the wave?
slides.explanation: Seven milliseconds, consistent with the light travel time between the two sites: gravitational waves move at the speed of light.

slides.heading: The collision, in Suns’ worth of mass
slides.note: Best estimates; the radiated mass is 3.0 ± 0.5 Suns

steps.label: Two black holes spiral together and merge
Ripples in space-time spread at light speed
Each 4 km laser arm stretches by a sliver
Both detectors record the same chirp

slides.alt: The northern arm of LIGO Hanford: a long, low, pale tunnel running straight to the horizon beside a road across dry grassland.
slides.caption: The northern arm of the Hanford detector. Each LIGO observatory is an L-shaped vacuum system 4 km long on each side.

slides.heading: A chirp you could hear
slides.text: In about eight cycles the signal rose from 35 to 250 hertz, which is in the range of human hearing, so it has been likened to a bird’s chirp. At its peak, the merger gave off more power than all the light from all the stars in the observable universe combined.

events.text: LIGO detects one, days before its formal run
Nobel Prize: Weiss, Barish and Thorne

slides.question: The signal is called GW150914. What does the name stand for?
slides.explanation: GW for gravitational wave, then the date it was seen: 2015-09-14. Einstein himself had doubted such tiny waves could ever be detected.
